analysis.one_liner: Swaps government review for employer promises to make hiring foreign guest farmworkers faster and cheaper.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 9, 2004 with zero cosponsors, the bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the government certification process for the H-2A farm guest worker program with employer-signed promises, which the Labor Department would have had to approve within 15 days after checking only for completeness. It would have replaced the special farm wage floor (the adverse effect wage rate) with a 51st-percentile prevailing wage that growers could document with their own surveys, let growers satisfy the housing rule with a cash allowance, cap penalties at $90,000 per application, and cut off federally funded legal aid to any immigrant who is not a current guest worker.
analysis.who_benefits: Crop growers, farm labor contractors, and grower associations. Guest-worker approvals would become near-automatic (15 days, completeness check only), the wage benchmark would drop from the adverse effect wage rate to the 51st-percentile prevailing wage, housing could be a cash allowance or waived by a governor's certification, penalties would be capped at $90,000 per application, one association application could cover many member farms, and state laws regulating the admission of foreign workers would be preempted. Guest workers themselves would gain a faster legal channel into these jobs, with codified guarantees for transportation reimbursement, a three-fourths employment guarantee, and back pay when shorted.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Crop growers and farm labor contractors

how_it_helps.text: Employers would file signed attestations instead of obtaining prior government certification of their recruitment of U.S. workers, and the Labor Department would have to issue approval within 15 days, reviewing only for completeness and obvious inaccuracies.

The required wage would drop from the adverse effect wage rate to the greater of the 51st-percentile prevailing wage or the state minimum wage, and an employer could rely on a prevailing-wage survey it or a group of employers conducted or funded.
The housing requirement could be satisfied with a cash allowance, or waived entirely in states whose governor certifies adequate migrant housing, and employer fees would be capped at $1,000.

Grower associations could file one application covering many member farms, transfer workers among those farms, and a violation would generally disqualify only the offending member rather than the whole association.

The bill would also codify some worker guarantees: reimbursement of long-distance transportation, a three-fourths employment-period guarantee, back pay when wages or benefits are shorted, civil penalties up to $15,000 for willfully displacing a U.S. worker, and disqualification from the program for violating employers.

Immigrants who previously violated their visa terms would be barred from guest worker status, but with a one-time waiver for anyone outside the United States, and the Department of Homeland Security would have to process petitions on an expedited basis.

analysis.who_pays: Farmworkers. The 51st-percentile prevailing wage would replace the higher adverse effect wage rate not only for guest workers but for U.S. workers in the same occupation at the same worksite, and employers could fund the wage survey used to set it. Enforcement would be weaker: penalties capped at $90,000 per application, approvals near-automatic, and the Legal Services Corporation barred from representing any alien who is not a current guest worker, with a 90-day mediation requirement before any damages suit on a guest worker's behalf. State and local laws regulating the admission of foreign workers would be preempted.

drawbacks.text: It replaces the adverse effect wage rate — a farm wage floor set from government wage surveys, designed to keep guest workers from undercutting U.S. farm pay — with the 51st-percentile prevailing wage, which by definition leaves roughly half of comparable local farm jobs paying more, and it lets employers rely on wage surveys that employers themselves funded.

Approval would become nearly automatic: the Labor Department must certify within 15 days and may review only for completeness and obvious inaccuracies, so the promises in the attestations would mostly be checked only after workers are already on the job.

Total civil penalties are capped at $90,000 per application, the Legal Services Corporation could no longer help any alien who is not a current H-2A worker, and any damages suit on behalf of a guest worker would first require 90 days of attempted federal mediation — leaving the most vulnerable farmworkers with the fewest ways to enforce the bill's own guarantees.

The honest supporter's case is that the existing certification process was slow and unpredictable enough that many growers avoided the program entirely, and that a usable legal channel is better for workers than hiring off the books; the bill does keep wage, housing, transportation, and employment guarantees on paper — but enforcement of those guarantees would rest on the same capped, after-the-fact administrative process the bill creates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real complaint — growers found the old approval process slow and uncertain — and it kept several worker guarantees in writing. But it paid for speed and predictability with a lower wage floor for some of the lowest-paid jobs in the country, near-automatic approvals, capped penalties, and reduced access to lawyers for the workers most likely to need them. On the bill's own terms, the trade runs mostly one way: toward growers' labor costs and away from worker wages and remedies.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, it never got a hearing or a vote and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Saxby Chambliss introduced the bill on March 9, 2004; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record — and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill would have replaced the labor certification process with employer attestations, with Labor Department approval due within 15 days after a check limited to completeness and obvious inaccuracies.
It would have replaced the adverse effect wage rate with a prevailing wage set at the 51st percentile of local farm wages, which employers could document using surveys they or other employers funded.

It would have capped civil penalties at $90,000 per application, barred the Legal Services Corporation from representing any alien who is not a current H-2A guest worker, and required 90 days of attempted mediation before a lawsuit on a guest worker's behalf.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: farmworkers kept the higher adverse-effect wage floor and legal-aid access of existing law, while growers missed their bid for faster, cheaper guest-worker hiring.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farmworkers kept existing protections; growers gained nothing

for.name: Saxby Chambliss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 9, 2004; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

for.name: Bush administration
for.what_they_did: That year publicly backed replacing H-2A labor certification with employer attestations and a prevailing-wage standard — the framework this bill carried.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the referred bill — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

against.name: United Farm Workers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the attestation-only approach, urging instead the bipartisan AgJOBS bill that paired guest-worker changes with legal status for undocumented farmworkers.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split ever showed itself.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (crop growers and farm labor contractors)
industries.note: The bill would give growers near-automatic guest-worker approvals, a lower wage benchmark, flexible housing rules, capped penalties, and preemption of state laws — savings that come out of wage floors and enforcement covering U.S. workers at the same worksites.

industries.industry: Grower associations acting as labor intermediaries
industries.note: One association application could cover many member farms, workers could be moved among members, and a violation would generally disqualify only the offending member — making large-scale guest-worker placement easier.

industries.industry: Federally funded legal aid (Legal Services Corporation grantees serving farmworkers)
industries.note: Legal aid would be barred from representing any alien who is not a current H-2A guest worker, and would need 90 days of attempted federal mediation before suing on a guest worker's behalf — cutting off counsel for the farmworkers least able to enforce wage laws.
